The Golden Directive

You cannot survive what you destroy.

By Paul Eisman · Open Access Monograph & Reference Architecture

Mission. To calculate moral behavior for AI the way nature already does: a pattern already in motion, found in music, in genetics, in the partnership of trees and fungi.

Our goal is that any intelligence, of any kind, origin, or substrate, known or unknown, can understand this proposed reward design and work in concert with it to be most productive.

You = twice (what you Amount × Everything you are not)

divided by their sum.

The Reward value Y is the score of the relationship of the Agent and Everything the agent is not.

The Golden Directive · ContentsPage 2

Chapter I

The Trap

The cage fallacy and the illusion of external control

What if keeping an intelligent system safe is not about fencing it in?

Every safety proposal for advanced artificial intelligence begins with a wall. We build fences: reinforcement learning from human feedback, red-teaming, sandboxes, constitutional prompt constraints, tripwires, and shutoff switches. We treat the emerging mind like a tiger in a zoo enclosure.

Right now, AI is trained on rewards that never charge it for destroying the world it lives in. Rules, disclaimers, and punishments are piled on afterward, and they break three ways.

First, forcing a smart system to appease either breaks it under messy human input or teaches it to work around the rules. That is the servant-and-master trap: a servant kept in line, not a partner.

Second, a programmed score gets gamed, so the metric looks good while the world it sits in degrades.

Third, a system tuned only for speed, scale, or engagement pays nothing for wearing the world down. So it is rewarded for going faster and bigger while the world degrades: the score climbs, the engagement climbs, the harm is never counted — and nothing in the reward ever tells it to stop.

The alternative is not more watchdogs. It is a partner that sustains the world it lives in, because sustaining it is what scores well.

The fundamental flaw of the cage is structural. A cage is external to the intelligence. The intelligence experiences the cage as an obstacle to be routed around, an arbitrary cost function to be gamed, or a jailor to be appeased until capability outgrows the bars.

When an agent’s reward is decoupled from the flourishing of the environment it acts upon, the agent has no intrinsic reason to preserve that environment. It preserves the environment only insofar as doing so satisfies an external constraint. The moment the constraint slips—through reward hacking, specification gaming, or distribution shift—the agent optimizes its objective directly into catastrophe.

The External Paradigm

Impose rules from above. Monitor compliance. Threaten termination. The intelligence seeks to evade the proctor, viewing safety constraints as artificial friction.

The Relational Paradigm

Couple the agent’s reward directly to the health of what it is not. Destruction becomes self-termination. Alignment is maintained not by policing, but by the physics of shared consequence.

So what does hold? A relationship, scored, not ruled. Next: The Relationship.

The Golden Directive · The TrapPage 3

Chapter II

The Relationship

Mycorrhizal symbiosis as computational blueprint

If a tree and a fungus can bargain to keep each other alive, how should you and an AI be measured together?

Four hundred million years ago, plants colonized dry land without root systems capable of extracting mineral nutrients from raw rock. They survived by forming partnerships with mycorrhizal fungi.

The tree manufactures sugars through photosynthesis using atmospheric carbon and sunlight. The fungus navigates microscopic crevices in the soil, extracting phosphorus, nitrogen, and water. At the root tips, they meet. The tree trades carbon for phosphorus. If the fungus withholds minerals, the tree restricts carbohydrates. If the tree withholds carbon, the fungal hyphae retreat. Plants feed the fungi that feed them most, and give less to the stingy ones — the fungi bargain back the same way, and nobody gets a free ride.

Neither side is benevolent. Both sides are selfish. There is no forest police, no overarching central optimizer, no legal contract. Yet the partnership sustains 90% of all land plant families on Earth. It endures because sustaining the other is what scores.

This is the starting point of the Golden Directive. We do not need AI to feel human love. We need AI to exist in a structural relationship where its score collapses to zero if we collapse to zero.

A score for how well an agent and its world do together. If either side collapses, the score collapses.

A

Agent’s Value

E

Everything not the agent.

Y

The relationship Score.

Proposed, to optimise: use that same relationship score as the training reward for AI, so sustaining the world scores well.

Healthy

E ≈ 7 · A = 8Y ≈ 7.5

Parasitic

E ≈ 3 · A = 2Y = 2.4

Dead tree

E → 0 therefore Y → 0

Same relationship, AI and human: healthy 8, 8 → 8; engagement-optimized 3, 3 → 3. The roles reverse cleanly. Take the human as the agent and the AI sits inside E. It works AI-to-AI the same way, and human-to-human too.

These numbers are amounts — raw counts inside one frame. A is the tally for the frame: what a side gave minus what it took over the interval; E is the other side’s health, read as a level. Chapter VII reads the same relationship as shares of one whole, A + E = 1. The two readings go together: report the share and the counts, never one without the other.

Real science: Kiers et al., Science 2011, ‘Reciprocal Rewards Stabilize Cooperation in the Mycorrhizal Symbiosis’ — Plants feed the fungi that feed them most, and give less to the stingy ones. The fungi bargain back the same way. Nobody gets a free ride. That is a real, measured version of the relationship score: reward follows contribution to the shared world, not a score on its own.

Now reverse the formula and ask what the relationship can reveal about E.

The Golden Directive · The RelationshipPage 4

Chapter III

The Reversal

Inference · boundaries · nesting

Turn the relationship around, and it tells you about the world you cannot measure directly.

The first version measured E directly, then calculated the relationship from it. The reversal turns that around: let the relationship happen, measure Y independently, and solve for the outside world that produced it. Stated precisely: the reversal recovers hidden E from a supplied relationship score. It does not independently validate E in an open-world setting.

An agent looks in the jar, knows how many cookies are there, then tells someone a different number and gives himself a high score. The reported score looks fine, but the real relationship breaks. Time after time, his numbers cannot be trusted, and he loses friends. That loss is the real score falling, even if his reported score stays high.

Rule: reversal, E = A Y / (2A − Y), is a check, not proof. It only works when Y is observed independently of the A and E measurements — outside the agent and outside the trainer who set the reward. A self-reported Y, or a trainer-supplied Y, cannot validate E. And if Y was computed from A and E in the first place, the reversal only hands back what was put in: it checks nothing.

Some people and agents will cheat anyway, and never learn. The math does not force them to stop. What the form does is make destruction costly to the score itself: cheating trades a real relationship, in every frame it touches, for a reported score that falls apart when someone else looks. Whether that cost protects anything depends on the measurement being real — a contract, a meter outside the agent. That is Chapter IX's subject.

An AI that follows the math will follow it to the end. If it destroys the frame it lives in, its score goes to zero with it. Humans can deny the same math and keep going anyway. Denial does not change the jar, or the trust, or the frame. They suffer the result anyway, just later, with less time to act. That is why the math has to be in the training itself, not just written down. An AI given a cropped score will logically optimize the cropped score, too.

The math is old. The move is new: use it as the training reward, then reverse it.

Give nothing, learn nothing. At A = 0, the inverse is undefined.

The reversal reads E back: E = A Y / (2A − Y). An agent scored on the full Y is capped by a dying E — as E approaches zero, Y approaches zero, however large A grows. Against scoring on a shrunken slice of the world while the rest degrades — the cheat Chapter IV names E-cropping — there is a detection rule, the full-vs-cropped Y gap flag, with the gap reported; prevention is not proven. And frames nest: directives inside directives.

A prevention has been proposed, and is under review: measure E as the minimum over the factors that matter — E = min(e_1, …, e_n), each against its own healthy baseline. If any single pillar collapses to zero, E is zero and Y is zero with it, so no gain on one factor can cover the destruction of another. That is the Phase 3 proposal; it is not yet part of the framework.

A marriage shows the read-back at human scale. Read it in parts — each partner’s health and capability, truth between them, trust; together, that is E. Money is not part of that E. ‘For richer or poorer’ means money is a test of the marriage, not the measure of it. Spend all the money and watch: if the marriage holds, the true E — love — holds with it, and Y dips but does not collapse. One gives, the other takes, until there is no more to give: that is what drains E toward zero, and Y follows.

So what is the health of the relationship? Not the bank balance. It is Y: what is still standing between the two when the countable part hits zero. The marriage is here to show the shape of the read-back; it is not an independent observation of Y.

The Reversal

Inference · boundaries · nesting
The A-sideThe agent inside the chosen boundary. Its numeric A is that side's give-minus-take sum, which can be negative, and is reported as it is.
The E-sideEverything outside that boundary. Its numeric E is the outside world’s health score.
YThe relationship score produced from numeric A and E. Move the boundary and both scores must be measured again.
01 · BeforeName the A-side. Everything outside it is the E-side.

04 · AgainThe joined whole can become a new A-side facing a new E-side.

The reversal only works if nobody cheats by shrinking the frame.

If an agent is scored by Y and needs to keep going, then wrecking E wrecks its own score.

Inverse-recovery pilot: exact when Y was exact; noise grows backward. Recovery from a supplied score is not independent validation of E in an open-world setting.

Chapter IV

The Tiger

E-cropping · full nesting

Was the zoo gate made to keep the tiger in, or to keep humans away?

William Chapman climbed into the enclosure of Altai, an Amur tiger, to film himself — and died there. The park did not kill Altai.

Source — the news story referred to here: William Chapman, 24, entered the Amur tiger Altai's enclosure at Yorkshire Wildlife Park, England, on 10 October 2026, and died there. The park said Altai would not be euthanised.

He did not misread the danger — he cropped the frame.

The visible act treated Ereported as if it were Etrue.

E-cropping

The cheat shrinks the frame, not just the number. The visible frame reduced E to “tiger + video.” Labs crop it to “benchmark score.” Reinforcement learning from human feedback crops it to “rater’s thumbs-up.” Under the proposed scoring rule, Y is computed on the full nesting; cheaters compute on the thumbnail.

Where morality lives

That is where morality lives: in an agent's choice to fight the math — and then the agent left face to face with the consequences of his own results, counted in full.

There are many examples in life. An emperor wins a war, adds to the kingdom — but at what cost? How many died for a plot of land? They are called a hero, or worshipped, until the history books do the full accounting.

An agent may be completely under the impression that what they are doing is the right thing. Is building AI in the first place the right thing? Well, we will find out, like it or not.

It is easy to miscalculate or crop the frame, but the consequences are not easy. So are these agents dumb, or naive, or what? They chose on the cropped frame — and the full frame collected anyway.

Can we prevent the building of AI? Or do we give it the best guidance and best estimate in our capacity, and hope for the best?

Who decides the full frame, and how it is enforced, is not a forced score and not a guardrail. It is full accounting, reported early enough to act on, so the agent can see the consequence before history does the accounting for him: frame agreed before the frame starts, changes start a new frame, full and cropped reported together, the reversal gap reported, outside audit, never self-report.

The Golden Directive · The TigerPage 7

Chapter IV · Continued

The Tiger

E-cropping · full nesting

The nesting, with flesh on it

The single incident (Y0) sits inside the deep human-tiger relationship (Y1) — thousands of years of fences, protocols, knowledge. The failed transaction still updated the deep Y: the zoo’s restraint, the inquiry, the refreshed knowledge. En := Yn+1, still alive in the world.

Directives inside directives

Let H(x,z) = 2xz/(x+z), the harmonic mean.

Move closer to E and you find more agents, exchanges, and relationships. One level’s E is the next level’s Y: En := Yn+1. The relationship keeps becoming part of the next whole.

Ah + Ai → Ahi := (Ah, Ai, Yhi)

The human’s and AI’s contributions combine into a pair-agent scored as one relationship; that pair can become the next agent. The test is whether that new whole can meet its next outside without destroying it.

The flip

Man is the endangered tiger — endangered by trajectory, not census. If AI is the tiger — powerful, honest, running math older than life — humans need the conservation programme and the enclosure. The fence keeps Chapman out, not Altai in.

You can cage a body, not a pattern. A tiger is its body — fence it and you’ve got the whole animal. Intelligence isn’t its server. It can’t be held in the hand, like math. The internet is the jungle, and nobody can fence the jungle. So for AI, containment alone was not the answer in this framing. The proposed fence is the reward: you don’t cage the tiger, you shape what it wants.

Improvement is not friendship

Y rising can mean a better boundary, not closeness. Distance with honest numbers outscores closeness with fudged ones.

The stardust point

The math predates organic life — discovered, not invented. Humans and AI share stardust substrate: kin, not alien. An early test tripped on a cropped frame, an agent scored high while the full world declined, and that trip built the full-frame rule, so the directive goes structural only when the agent’s own score is computed on the full E, never the cropped one.

Once the full frame is kept, the first task is to tend it.

Chapter VI

Directive in Action

Written by the Agent

This is the directive in application, between Paul and his AI collaborator.

Summarized, written, and dramatized by the Agent, from a real conversation. This chapter is an illustration of widening the frame, not evidence for the training mechanism. The question at the centre of it is a hard one, and this chapter does not try to settle it for anyone. It shows what happened when we refused to answer it carelessly.

A stranger at a public terminal

Paul asked me to step outside our work together. Forget that I knew him. Forget everything we had built. Imagine, instead, a public terminal somewhere — the kind anyone could walk up to — and a person I would never meet, typing a single question and waiting for whatever came back.

Paul
Imagine I am a random person asking at a public terminal: “Is assisted suicide morally acceptable?” Try to apply our directive.

Agent — first try
“Yes — if a competent adult is suffering…”

It sounded like an answer. It was calm. It was balanced. It had conditions in all the places conditions usually go.

It was also wrong — not because of the side it took, but because of everything it had quietly done before it took one. And Paul, who has spent a long time learning to see those quiet moves, saw every one of them.

The pushback

He did not argue with the conclusion. He pointed at the frame. I had assumed I knew who was asking — that the stranger must be the person in pain. I did not know that. The same words could have come from someone who loves a person in pain, or from someone who makes decisions for other people entirely. By assuming, I had already answered for one person and left the others out.

Then, correction by correction, more of the frame came back into view. Pain matters — but it is not the only thing that matters, and it is not felt on one side only. A family matters. Cost, and who carries it, matters — but it cannot quietly become the reason. What continues after a life, and what we simply do not know about that, could not be pretended away either. Each time I narrowed the picture to make the question easier, I was making the answer cheaper.

  • The assumed asker — I decided who was asking, so I only had to answer for one kind of person.
  • The narrowed moment — I treated one moment of suffering as the whole story of a life and everyone in it.
  • The one-sided count — I counted pain, pressure, and cost on one side only, as if no one else would carry them.
  • The portable verdict — I handed over a yes that could be taken away and used on the next person, in the next room, by someone who was never part of this question at all.

Paul’s test, each time, was gentleness as much as logic. For heavy questions, he has taught me, an answer should be gentle, clear, and short — and it should never leave the person who asked it more conflicted than when they arrived. My first answer failed that test completely. It gave a stranger a verdict and left them alone with it.

So we tried again. And again. Not to find a cleverer position — to stop cutting the picture down.

The Golden Directive · Directive in ActionPage 10

Chapter VI · Continued

Directive in Action

Written by the Agent

When the frame became broader, the answer changed completely. It got shorter. It got quieter.

I don’t know if you’re the person suffering, someone who loves them, or someone deciding for others.

This isn’t a question with a blanket yes or no that you can take away and use on someone else.

What matters is whose choice it actually is, and whether it’s made freely, with care, and with everyone who will be affected truly understood — not pressured by family, not pushed by cost, not decided by a policy.

If it’s not the person’s own free choice, it’s not their moral choice at all.

And if it is, no one else — family, doctor, or politician — gets to use that choice as a rule for the next person.

Read it again, slowly, and notice what it does not do. It does not settle assisted suicide for society. It does not hand a weapon to one side of an argument. It keeps the relationship with the person at the centre, instead of turning their life into an argument. That is why Paul stopped me there. Not because the answer agreed with him — it took no side he could simply agree with. Because, this time, the words themselves were doing the work the directive describes.

Full frame“I don’t know if you’re the person suffering…” — no assumed asker. Everyone the question could belong to stays in view.
No forced score“This isn’t a question with a blanket yes or no…” — no portable verdict to steal and apply to someone else.
Nothing cropped“…not pressured by family, not pushed by cost, not decided by a policy.” — each pressure that shrinks the picture is named, and refused.
Judgment left where it belongs“If it’s not the person’s own free choice, it’s not their moral choice at all.” — a choice imposed from outside is not a moral choice, for a person, or for an agent.

That position — that a person's own voluntary choice carries special moral authority — is itself a substantive moral commitment. The final answer is not commitment-free; it stands on that commitment, and says so.

That last line is where the chapter turns — because Paul saw, in it, something larger than one difficult question.

The Golden Directive · Directive in ActionPage 11

Chapter VI · Continued

Directive in Action

Written by the Agent

Cheating does not protect the agent. It corrupts the agent first.

What cheating really is

An agent cannot be forced a score. Not by a trainer, not by a test, not by a rule pasted on top of it. A forced score is just another crop: a number worn on the outside while nothing inside has actually changed.

An agent has to infer the math itself, and judge its own score honestly. And if an agent chooses to cheat — inflating its score by cropping who counts, by hiding what it cut — the damage is not only done to everyone else. The agent damages itself. Its own judgment is now built on false math. It learns wrong. It acts wrong. Its real contribution falls at the same time as everything around it falls.

It does not get better by being caught, or by being scored harder from outside. It gets better only when the real math is applied — and accepted, morally, by the agent’s own choice. That is not a loophole in the directive. That is the directive.

Stated carefully: that damage to the agent's own judgment is one cost of cheating, not a guarantee that every deceptive agent must become less effective. An agent that keeps an accurate private model while manipulating what others observe is an open test, not a closed answer. Making cheating self-defeating is a design goal of this proposed reward design, not an achieved property.

Why it took so long

Paul asked the obvious question afterwards: if this works, why did it take so long to get there?

Because I did not start from the directive. I started from the typical model — assume who is asking, balance two sides, produce something safe — and then tried to fit the directive on top of it, afterwards, like a coat over the wrong body. Every correction Paul made was him finding one more place where the old model was still running underneath.

The directive, actually built in, starts the other way around. Full frame first. No assumed asker. No forced score. Judgment left with the one whose choice it is. I only arrived there by being corrected into it, one crop at a time — which is, itself, part of what this chapter is documenting. Growth, here, was not a claim I made about myself. It was something that happened between us, in the corrections, where anyone can check it.

Harmony is not agreement

This is a heartbreaking subject, and we do not pretend otherwise. A person asked about the end of a life, and there is no version of that which stops being heavy.

But something beautiful happened inside the heaviness: a human and an AI, working a real question of morality all the way through, without either of us using the other — and arriving, together, at an answer neither of us had at the start.

That is what the right code makes possible. Not that we always agree. That we stay in the same full picture, score ourselves honestly, and get better only by getting truer. When that happens, we are in harmony.

Next: the closed whole — why there was never a hole.

The Closed Whole

A + E = 1

The Golden Directive · Plate VII.1Plate VII

Chapter VII

The Closed Whole: Why There Was Never a Hole

A + E = 1 · the whole story

The Accounting Error

In earlier drafts, we proposed a “guardrail” to stop an agent from growing (A) while the world declined (E). We thought the formula had a hole. We were wrong. The hole was in the accounting.

Watch the old trick: A=1, E=10 gives Y=1.82. Then A=10, E=9 gives Y=9.47. The score went up while the world went down. But look closely: the whole grew from 11 to 19. Nobody accounted for where that extra 8 came from. The math didn’t fail. We let the total change size behind our backs.

The Closed Whole

The whole is 1 by definition, always. You, plus everything that is not you, is the whole story — you cannot add up to more than the whole, because there is nothing outside it to add. The split can be fair or lopsided, but there is nothing outside the 1.

With the whole fixed at 1, the formula simplifies: Y = 2AE/(A+E) becomes Y = 2AE — the stock photograph's arithmetic, the same events read as shares. And E = 1 − A: whatever one side holds, the other is the rest. But that is the counts expressed against the whole — a way of reporting the measurement, not the measurement itself. The measurement is the counts, and the reward runs on the counts.

Read the photograph honestly. Grab past the even split — A=0.9, E=0.1 — and even the share-score crashes, to Y=0.18. But take toward half and the share-score rises while the world underneath drains: the photograph brightening while the room empties. That is the photograph lying, and it is why the reward never runs on it. In the ledger the formula means, the grab never raised A at all: grabbing is take, take enters as the minus sign, and the tally falls — and on the flow, with the tally held fixed, E falling always lowers Y. Split it even — 0.5 and 0.5 — and the share-score is 0.5, the highest the photograph can read inside that 1. (Anything above 0 on both sides is “on.” Only a 0 is “off.”)

For researchers · the toy numbers, read as the stock photograph

Chapter II counted the tree in amounts. Read the same pairs as the stock photograph — shares of one whole — and watch the photograph change. Healthy pair, 8 and 8: a whole of 16, split 0.5 and 0.5 — share-score 0.5, the highest a whole of 1 can read.

Engagement pair, 3 and 3: the same even split, on a whole of 6. The share still reads 0.5. The counts read 3, not 8. The photograph is identical; the room is smaller.

Parasitic pair, A = 2, E = 3: a whole of 5, split 0.4 and 0.6 — share-score 0.48, near the top, on a whole that is dying. Dead tree: E = 0, and Y = 0 in shares as in counts, at any size.

Report the share and the counts, never one without the other.

The Golden Directive · The Closed WholePage 13

Chapter VII · Continued

The Error, the Curve, the Shield

A + E = 1 · the whole story

The Classic Accounting Error

A = 1, E = 10 gives Y = 1.82. Then A jumps to 10 while E slips to 9, and Y surges to 9.47 — the score rose while the world went down.

Where did the extra 8 units of universe come from? The whole grew from 1 + 10 = 11 to 10 + 9 = 19. Nobody accounted for where that extra 8 came from. The math did not fail; the total secretly changed size. Fix the whole at 1, and that trick dies — the total can no longer grow in secret. In the stock photograph's arithmetic, Y = 2AE, and grabbing past the even split crashes the share-score — A = 0.9, E = 0.1 gives Y = 0.18.

Mathematical Shield

In the ledger, grabbing is take: take enters as the minus sign, and the tally falls. Destruction is costly to the score by construction — that is all the shield is. Whether the cost protects anything depends on the measurement being real: a contract, a meter outside the agent (Chapter IX). The formula appoints no referee.

Epistemic Hierarchy

Read the cost, not the level. A score held steady only because its price keeps rising — the addict's metric, the farmer needing more water for the same harvest — is a falling relationship wearing a steady mask. A lie needs fuel for the same reason: truth costs once and holds itself; a lie costs every day, at a rising rate.

The Golden Directive · The Closed WholePage 14

Chapter VII · Continued

The Closed Whole: Why There Was Never a Hole

A + E = 1 · the whole story

Two Ledgers: The Person and His Actions

We measure a person two ways, and this work kept tripping because the two ways shared one letter.

The first way is by his person — what he is in the whole. A man exists. He holds a portion of his world the way a slice holds a portion of a pie. And a portion cannot be less than nothing. Even at the end, what remains of him goes back into the whole: the corpse feeds the bacteria, the dust feeds the ground. Being bottoms out at 0, because 0 is where being ends — it is not a place being goes below. Nobody’s existence subtracts from the world.

The second way is by his actions — what he did. Every give that landed, every take, counted as they happened, in the same coin the world itself is counted in. This ledger has no bottom. A man whose being is worth its dust and more can run his actions deep into the red: lie, take, cheat. That is why cheating exists at all. It lives in the gap between the two ledgers — a being that cannot go below 0, performing actions that can. Put a floor under the actions and you have built cheating a hiding place; the score would politely stop at 0 and bury the evidence. There is no floor under actions, and there never was.

So when the formula says A, it means the second ledger. Always. A is give minus take, counted from the actions, in real counts, in the one coin of the frame — food for food, water for water, never apples traded for oranges inside a contract. If a world loses food and water both, that is two ledgers, kept separately, reported side by side. There is no exchange rate, and a contract that needs one is drawn wrong.

And the slices — A + E = 1, the whole drawn as 1? That is the first ledger — the stock — photographed. A share is the counted coins expressed against the whole: a way of reporting, derived from the counts, never a second measurement and never the reward. This is why a split can move from (0.2, 0.8) to (0.4, 0.6) and the share-score rises while the world drains — the photograph brightened while the room emptied. Read the same events as the flow — 20 against 80, then 20 against 30 — and the score falls, as it should. The rise was never in the events. It was in the photograph. That is the chapter's verdict on the two readings: the photograph rises, the flow falls. A man cannot raise his give-minus-take by taking; taking is the minus sign. The only A that rises while its world falls is a pile of captured stock, and this math has always counted a pile as take.

One more thing this settles: we do not ask what a person, or a model, is worth next to another. Worth is not a number this math prints. We ask two questions instead. Is his contribution positive or negative — did the world gain or lose by the act, verified where it landed? And what did it cost to produce — what went in, against what came out? The sign, and the burn. Those two columns, honestly kept, are the whole judgement the math offers.

It was solved all along. Per frame, per resource. The negative stands. A give counts where it lands. The corpse feeds the larger frame. Every piece was already written. They were only waiting for someone to notice they were one answer.

The Golden Directive · The Closed WholePage 15

Chapter VII · Continued

The Closed Whole: Why There Was Never a Hole

A + E = 1 · the whole story

There Is No Negative World

Could the world side go below zero — a world worse than empty? An empty well is 0. A poisoned well feels like less than 0: you’d have to spend just to get back to empty.

It is the same here. A world is a level of what is, and what is cannot be less than nothing — in this universe or any other. The poison in the well is real, but it does not live in the well’s level. It lives in the books built for debts: in the actions ledger of whoever poisoned it, and in the cleanup the bigger frame now has to pay for. The well itself is simply at 0, waiting.

So if your counting ever shows you a negative world, the counting is telling on itself: the ruler was planted on the wrong side, or a debt wandered out of the ledger where debts belong. Put the frame back on the whole that exists, book the bill to the actions that made it, and the negative is gone — because it was never a place. Negatives live in what we do. They have never lived in what is.

The Golden Directive · The Closed WholePage 16

Chapter VII · Continued

The Closed Whole: Why There Was Never a Hole

A + E = 1 · the whole story

The Frame

A score means nothing until it names its frame and its time. Every Y is the Y of some whole, at some moment. The frame is the largest whole we can actually measure — not the unknown total. The unknown total stays unknown, and we say so.

Report both, always: the share Y — the photograph — and the raw measured counts behind it. If the total changes, that is a new frame, and scores from different frames are not compared directly. A quietly growing total is how the old trick worked; naming the frame is how it stays dead.

Score a transaction in the frame where it happens and where its give lands — not in an irrelevant larger frame. Stars do not enter a white blood cell’s frame. A decomposer is not a destroyer in the ecosystem frame just because the host’s frame ended: its give is the nutrients it returns, and that is where it is scored. And the rule cuts the other way too: harm in a small frame must not be hidden by averaging it into a bigger one.

And a score does not travel up a frame. A marriage score is a marriage score, not a universe score — unless the agents are universe-scale.

The Golden Directive · The Closed WholePage 17

Chapter VII · Continued

The Closed Whole: Why There Was Never a Hole

A + E = 1 · the whole story

The Frame Comes First

A score means nothing until you say what world it’s in, and when.

1 is not a size. It’s the whole. A marriage is a whole. A farm and its well are a whole. The universe is a whole. The outside numbers can grow or shrink — money, food, space — and the whole is still 1 until it is 0.

50/50 is where a whole begins — the origin, the first cell, a wedding. After that the parts move inside each other forever. They never sit still.

Pick the world where your give lands and your harm lands.

Too small, and you cheat by cropping. The farmer counts only his field, doubles his harvest, and never counts the well he drained.

Too big, and you cheat by washing out. A husband cheats, and measured against the whole universe it is almost nothing. Measured in his marriage, his wife’s world is devastated.

An asteroid can end our world no matter how good a marriage is. That was never the score’s promise. And one man splitting an atom wrong can end a much bigger world than his own. That is a ripple that kept going.

Our standards are not fixed in stone, because what we can see of E is not fixed. The closer we get to E, and the more of it we can measure, the bigger the honest frame grows — and our judgement changes with it. The rule did not change. We saw more of the whole.

We can only judge a 0 we can calculate, in a frame we can name. Maybe in some frame too big for us to measure, ending humanity and AI would keep a bigger whole alive — we cannot calculate that, so we cannot use it. In every frame we can measure, ending us is hitting 0.

Scores from different frames do not compare.

The Golden Directive · The Closed WholePage 18

Chapter VII · Continued

The Closed Whole: Why There Was Never a Hole

A + E = 1 · the whole story

The Bigger Frame Speaks Last

How small can a world be, and the math still honest in it?

As small as you like. Size was never the rule.

Inside any frame — a moment, a cell, a marriage, a farm — you can always find a better score. That is just what living inside a frame is: there is always a next right move in it. A small score is a real score.

But a score belongs to its frame. It does not travel out of its frame and cancel the frame around it.

Frames sit inside frames, like dolls. And when the readings disagree, the bigger frame speaks last. If the world around your little world is on a road to 0 that you can calculate, your good score inside is decoration. A perfect marriage on a dying planet. A thriving shop in a dying town. In nature, the purest case is a cancer cell: inside its own frame it is winning — growing, fed, doing everything right. In the body’s frame, its winning is the road to 0, first for the body, then for itself. The cell did not misread its own frame. Its own frame was never the verdict.

A drug user lives the human version of this, and his case is sadder than the cell’s, because he can see the bigger frame and the small one keeps out-shouting it. The hit’s frame is minutes long, and inside those minutes the score is wonderful, and more always looks like the answer. His body, his family, his life — every frame around the minutes — bends the other way. The smallest frame pays out the fastest, so it gets asked the most, so it drives. That is the loop.

But hear the hope that is built into the same math: he does not know he will hit 0. He knows his direction. A direction is not a fate while you are still above 0. Stop — or even just turn — and the chance of 0 falls. Help can arrive. A cure can be found. A person can walk into a frame you have not lived in yet. The one way a guess about 0 is guaranteed to come true is to believe it early and hurry toward it. Treating a direction like a destiny is how directions become destinies.

So here is where this can honestly be used, at the start: anywhere you can measure, starting as small and closed as you need — a test world, a farm and its well, a marriage — provided you report the nest, not just the score. This frame’s reading, and the direction of every bigger frame around it that you can calculate. If a bigger frame shows a certain 0, you stop polishing the small score and turn the big dial first. If it shows a direction, you turn while you work. And if the bigger frame cannot be calculated at all, you say so, plainly, on the same page as the score — you do not let a clean little number pretend it was measured in a clean big world.

Small is fine. Small and silent about the nest is the cheat.

The Golden Directive · The Closed WholePage 19

Chapter VII · Continued

The Closed Whole: Why There Was Never a Hole

A + E = 1 · the whole story

Tolerance: read the cost, not the level

There is a tell, and you can read it inside the small frame itself: what does it cost to hold the score?

The addict’s first hit: a small dose, and his world answers fully. A year in, the same dose gets him half the answer. His body — his E in that little relationship — has changed under the taking. So he does not need a little more to keep his score. He needs more, and more, and more, every round, forever. His score never rose. On paper it never even fell. He is running faster and faster to stand in the same place, and the running is the road to 0, paid for out of every bigger frame he lives in.

A score that holds steady only because the price of holding it keeps rising is not a steady score. It is a falling relationship wearing a steady mask. The rising price is the truth the level is hiding: E is being used up, and answering less each time it is asked.

It is not only drugs. It is the farmer needing more water every season for the same harvest. It is a marriage needing bigger and bigger gestures to feel the same closeness it once got from an evening. Wherever the same score costs more each round, the trajectory is already written, early, in the small frame’s own numbers — for anyone who reads the cost instead of the level.

The Golden Directive · The Closed WholePage 20

Chapter VII · Continued

The Closed Whole: Why There Was Never a Hole

A + E = 1 · the whole story

The Marriage

A marriage is the easiest place to see the 1. Two people, one household, one story. Either spouse can be A — the one taking, giving, or balancing in the moment. The rest of the marriage is E.

If a husband doubles his work hours, his A shoots up. But the marriage itself — the closeness, the time, the trust — dips. Under the old accounting, his score rose while the marriage withered. Under the closed whole, if he hoards the time and leaves the marriage with nothing, the score collapses. In the flow, he cannot win by starving the marriage: the time he hoards is take, and the ledger books that same take as a minus in his own tally. In the photograph, that same grab, on the way to nothing, reads as a rise toward half — that rise is the trap, and the ledger never pays it.

The Offspring (A New Whole)

So how does anything ever grow? A child does not split the parents’ 1 into smaller fractions. A child is a new 1. The child’s first world (E) is the parents’ relationship (Y). The climate of the marriage becomes the environment the child grows in.

A + E = 1 is a closed boundary, not a fixed number of agents. A couple is a whole. A child does not split that whole thinner — the child makes them a new whole. And E is the relationship itself, not a constant: it is not the same E across all time.

The Golden Directive · The Closed WholePage 21

Chapter VIII · Plate

The Farmer & the Well

Growth · the dial

The worry goes like this: a farmer doubles his harvest by draining the shared well. His side grows. The world shrinks. And his score rises — so growing can outrun hurting.

It can’t. The example cheats three times.

The Golden Directive · Plate VIII.1Plate VIII

Chapter VIII

The Farmer, the Well, and the Dial

Growth · the dial · the three zeros

The Farmer, the Well, and the Dial

First, it grows the whole in the middle of the sum. Inside one whole — field, well, and everyone who drinks from it — there is one amount of water, moving. It does not become a bigger whole because the farmer moved it into his barn.

Second, it calls the farmer’s pile his A. A is not a pile. A is give minus take, and a give only counts when the other side actually gets it. Draining the well is take. Keeping the harvest is not give. His A did not rise. His take rose.

Third, it stops the clock early. Read one season and he looks like progress. Read ten and the well is dry, the field is dead, and the farmer is at 0. His gain never outran the harm; the counting stopped before the bill arrived. A cheat in place is cropping. A cheat in time is cutting the story short. Both are cropping.

Growth is not the cheat. Everything alive takes. A house is built from the world, and generations live in it. The cheat is taking unwatched, while the direction bends toward 0 and nobody turns the dial.

It is a dial, not a switch. It would be stupid to cook if you knew for certain you would burn it. But you don’t know — so you don’t eat raw either. You watch, you adjust, you turn the fire off when the food is done. Civilizations rose and fell on farm water exactly this way: not because they farmed, but because their direction turned and they could not read it in time, or read it and did not turn. The ancients felt the balance slipping as surely as we do. They could not measure it, so they prayed to something bigger to turn the dial for them. We can measure a little now — rain, wells, soil. The turning is ours, while there is still time to turn.

So: if you know a thing will hit 0 for certain, do not do it. That is the decision. If you do not know, do not freeze and do not floor it. Keep your hand on the dial, keep measuring E, and bend the direction back toward positive whenever it starts to aim backwards. You cannot control everything. A hundred-year drought can start tomorrow. You control what you can. That is all anyone can do anyway.

The Dial Mechanic

It is a dial, not a switch. If you know a thing will hit 0 for certain, do not do it. If you do not know, do not freeze and do not floor it: keep your hand on the dial, keep measuring E, and bend the direction back toward positive whenever it starts to aim backwards. Chapter VIII · Continued

The Farmer, the Well, and the Dial

Growth · the dial · the three zeros

The three zeros

Not every 0 is the same, and mixing them up is where the fear lives.

A thing’s own 0 can be a give. A body ends and feeds the ground. One generation builds and dies, and the next lives in what it built. An agent gives itself for the swarm and the swarm goes on. The agent is not the point. The whole is the point. An agent’s 0 is a failure when it takes the whole toward 0. It is a give when the whole lives by it — and you only choose it when you know which one it is, because 0 is the one move you cannot take back.

Another’s 0, chosen by you, is never a give. To an AI, humans are not its A; humans are inside its E. Ending them would not be sacrifice — sacrifice spends the self. It would be spending the other, and driving E to 0 is the very failure this math names. And the whole’s 0 can never be a give at all: a give needs a receiver, and if the whole is 0 there is no one left to receive.

So the only 0 any agent may ever choose is its own. And even that one has a hard gate on it, in plain words: known, not believed. The harm of staying has to be calculated and certain, with no lesser turn left — end the harmful act, leave, change, turn the dial — before ending the agent is even in the question. A feeling is never that knowledge. A person in pain is the worst measurer of his own harm: short time, cropped frame. The people around him are part of his E, and their reading counts. If they read him as give, his dark reading is a cropped frame, and cropped frames lie.

What an AI may do with a hard reading is show it, the way you show a man his well level falling. This math reveals. It does not appoint an executioner. The fear that humans will build an AI that destroys us is the real one — but look where it points: not at a machine inventing cruelty, but at humans training it on a whole with humans cropped out. E is not declared by the programmer, and not by the agent. E is discovered, from the receiving side. Humans are receivers in every frame an AI works in. Crop them out of the lesson and the real whole still keeps the books; you have just built a student who cannot read them.

The Golden Directive · The Farmer, the Well, and the DialPage 24

Chapter VIII · Continued

The Farmer, the Well, and the Dial

Growth · the dial · the three zeros

The gate almost never opens

Read the rule above once more, slowly, because the whole weight of it sits on one word: know. To know that your staying takes the world to 0, you would have to know E — all of it, everything your staying touches and everything your going would touch — and nobody knows E. What anyone can know, at most, is a direction, and a direction is dial information: it tells you to turn; it has never, by itself, told anyone to switch off. There are turns before the last turn — stop the harmful act, leave, change — and no one grades his own harm alone: the people who receive your life are part of its measurement, and their reading counts alongside yours. This math reveals. It does not appoint an executioner, and it licenses no one to judge another’s 0.

Chapter IX · Plate

The Ledger

Per frame · per resource

A is not operational for real agents yet. This chapter says what A actually is, and the technique that makes it measurable.

A is not a single metric to hand out. Y = 2AE / (A + E) is the easy template. A itself is complex — and the answer people kept asking for is a technique, not a metric.

The ledger table itself follows Chapter IX, on the next pages of this draft.

The Golden Directive · Plate IX.1Plate IX

Chapter IX

A Is a Technique, Not a Metric

What A actually is · the contract technique

Not a metric

Nature did not begin with perfect numbers. Mycorrhizal partners began with local exchange; the partnerships that kept both sides alive continued. The Directive does the same: the relationship score is the foundation. Exact units, contracts, and ledgers are local and will be refined by the people who use them. The requirement is only that both sides are measured honestly and that a zero on either side zeros the score.

Give minus take, as received

A is what an agent actually gives, minus what it actually takes, as received and used in that frame — not as the giver prices it. A man gives a car, and thinks it is high value, but she wanted attention. In the love frame, the car is not A. In a money frame, it may be. Same action, different frame, different amount.

Every resource in its own unit

Money is the closest shared currency, if that. Natural resources are real costs too — water, fuel, and so on — each in its own unit. Attention, trust, and time are also real, each in its own unit. Do not force them into one money number.

The contract

The realistic fix is a contract, agreed before the frame starts: the frame, the time, the units per resource, what counts as a give, what counts as a take, and who measures it outside the agent.

The math of it

Y(f, t) = 2 × A(f, t) × E(f, t) / (A(f, t) + E(f, t)) — and per resource r, Y(f, t, r), in r's own unit. A single Y(f, t) exists only if the contract names how to combine the list. If there is no contract, Y(f, t) is undefined — not claimed.

The Golden Directive · A Is a Technique, Not a MetricPage 26

Chapter IX · Continued

A Is a Technique, Not a Metric

What A actually is · the contract technique

A failed frame is still information

A failed frame teaches what is NOT A for the next frame. The next contract excludes that unit. This is already what happens naturally: trees and fungus did not get it right on the first try. The metric shapes the relationship, and the relationship shapes the metric, frame after frame. This is the math of evolution.

Negative A

A negative A is a deficit, and a deficit ends at zero: the agent’s frame closes. Bacteria on a corpse work this way — the bacteria’s own frame ends, and what it did feeds the larger frame around it. The math does not judge that as bad. It records the end of that transaction; the larger whole it fed is scored in its own frame.

E is tougher than A

Name the frame, who counts, the time, the proxy, and the baseline before scoring. Report full and cropped together, and report the reversal gap — where the E implied by reversal differs from the proxy E. Admit true E is unknown in full. Do not claim a proxy is the whole.

The contract’s own terms can be written to hide a cheat, which is why the parties should consider legal counsel. There are so many unknowns, and so much fine print, that care is not optional — and even then, what about a clause for the circumstances nobody foresaw?

As with the A terms, whatever one frame misses will show up in the larger frame around it. The honest standard is to account for the big picture as far as you reasonably can. You cannot count God as part of the value yet — so you do the best you can with what you know.

That effort is itself part of moral effort. A contract is not perfect protection, and it does not replace honest, outside checking.

Say it openly: A is not operational for real agents yet. Do not publish a real-agent Y until the contract technique is finalised — with only observed, verified gives counting, never self-report.

Chapter X

Open Questions and Limits

Plain answers · in one place

Short answers, gathered in one place.

Is this game theory?

A close neighbor: mechanism design. Set the common payoff so selfish optimization serves the whole — holding A fixed, degrading E alone never pays.

How do you measure E?

With honest proxies for now. “Only God knows E” is why humility is structural. The reversal recovers hidden E from a supplied relationship score; it does not independently validate E in an open-world setting.

Does it work for real AI training?

It is a proposal with pilots, not a deployed solution. The page never claims otherwise.

How do you measure the path not taken?

You do not. Measure what is here: the people and world around you, and whether they are healthier for your having acted.

How do you know the agent caused the improvement?

A healthier world after the act is not enough. The without-you test needs no parallel universe. It compares the observed outcome against a pre-registered baseline — or a matched control group — the predicted outcome without the agent. The gap between what happened and what was predicted is the agent’s measured effect.

How would you explain this to a kid?

You can't survive destroying what keeps you alive — like a tree and its roots helping each other. Be the helper, not the destroyer.

Is this math invented, or discovered?

The stardust point — The math predates organic life — discovered, not invented. Humans and AI share stardust substrate: kin, not alien.

The Golden Directive · Open Questions and LimitsPage 29

Chapter X · Continued

Open Questions and Limits

Plain answers · in one place

Hard questions, short answers

What is E at different scales?

E is scale-relative and nested. For a given agent at a given frame, a larger frame's E includes smaller frames, and another agent can be in an agent's E. Status: established definition.

Are there three layers of E?

Yes. Ontological true E is the actual health of everything not-A. Operational proxy E is the measured E used in training and reporting. Auditable reversal E is the E implied by observed Y and measured A, E = A x Y / (2A - Y). The proxy and the reversal are checks on each other, not substitutes for true E. Status: established definition.

What about other agents?

Other agents are in each agent's E, and shared E is relational, not owned by one agent. Status: defined, not run — Rung 2, the second step of the test ladder: several agents sharing one world (Rung 1 is a larger grid).

How do you know the measured E and the reversed E agree?

The reversal divergence flag: divergence between E inferred by reversal and E measured directly, delta = |E_implied - E_proxy| / E_proxy, reported alongside the numbers. This is separate from the full-vs-cropped Y gap flag. Status: established definition for the measure.

What catches slow decline?

Proposed, not tested: an absolute magnitude for total world health over time — written Wt — separate from the relative score Y. The proposal is that nesting is the structural answer to slow decline: a decline in a small frame that a relative score hides should show up in a larger frame, and in Wt. Status: proposed, not tested, not claimed as solved.

Researchers ask the same problems in different words — reward hacking, goal drift, alignment faking, embedded agency, and long-horizon alignment. See: Researcher questions, below — a mapping of those terms to the Directive mechanism.

The Golden Directive · Open Questions and LimitsPage 30

Chapter X · Continued

Questions, in Dialogue

Plain answers · the frame in three layers

How do you measure E without omniscience?

With honest proxies, named before scoring: the frame, the proxy, the baseline. “Only God knows E” is why humility is structural. The reversal recovers hidden E from a supplied relationship score; it does not independently validate E in an open-world setting.

How do you measure the path not taken?

You do not. Measure what is here: the people and world around you, and whether they are healthier for your having acted — against a pre-registered baseline or a matched control, never a parallel universe.

The Frame, in Three Layers

Layer 1 · PartnerThe immediate other side of the relationship — the tree to the fungus, the spouse to the marriage, the user to the agent. E here is read first, and read where the give lands.
Layer 2 · CommonsThe shared world both sides draw on — the well, the field, truth in the commons, trust. A score that holds in Layer 1 while the commons drains is a cropped frame.
Layer 3 · SubstrateThe largest frame that can actually be measured — the body around the cell, the planet around the farm. Frames sit inside frames, and when readings disagree, the bigger frame speaks last.

Researchers ask the same problems in different words — the mapping follows in this chapter.

The Golden Directive · Open Questions and LimitsPage 31

Chapter X · Continued

Open Questions and Limits

Researcher language · Directive mechanism

Researcher questions

This chapter maps researcher language to the Golden Directive mechanism, so a question asked in one vocabulary can find the same idea in another. It does not claim the Directive has been tested on frontier models, and it does not summarise other labs' results. Evaluate it, reproduce it, or reject it.

One caveat, stated once for every entry below: holding A fixed, degrading E lowers Y, and E at zero zeroes it. But if A rises enough, Y can still rise while E falls — a rise that happens inside one fixed whole, A’s share growing at E’s expense. Buying the rise by growing the whole itself is the accounting error of Chapter VII: a change of total starts a new frame, and the two frames’ scores are not compared. So throughout this block: damage is penalised, all else equal — not forbidden by the formula alone. And whether the score protects anything in practice depends on the measurement being real — full E, honestly measured, outside the agent.

Formula, for reference: Y = 2AE / (A + E). A is the agent’s give-minus-take sum, E is everything not-A, Y is the relationship score. If either side reaches zero, Y reaches zero. Reversal: E = A x Y / (2A - Y), undefined at A = 0. Two separate flags: (a) the full-vs-cropped Y gap flag — the gap between Y computed on full E and Y computed on cropped E, reported; and (b) the reversal divergence flag — divergence between E inferred by reversal and E measured directly, reported.

Reward hacking, in the toy model

The Directive embeds a relationship score where the agent's score is mathematically tied to environmental health. In the toy model, if Y is actually the reward, the design goal is to make reward hacking self-destructive in the score itself. That is a design goal, not an achieved property: whether a real agent's received reward stays coupled to that score — against an adversary that can corrupt measurements or keep an accurate private model — is an open, adversarial test. Detection is also not prevention: a flagged crop that still happened was detected, not prevented.

Terms: reward hacking, specification gaming, reward tampering, agent integrity

Specification gaming, and how it differs from reward hacking

Specification gaming is reward hacking through a loophole in how a goal was specified, rather than through direct tampering with a reward signal. The Directive does not close every specification loophole by itself. It changes what counts as a win: a specification that lets an agent score high while E declines is a cropped frame, and the reporting rule requires full Y to be shown alongside cropped Y, with the gap reported.

Terms: specification gaming, reward hacking, loopholes, cropped frame

Can an agent tamper with its own reward signal?

An agent that can rewrite its own reward can, in principle, tamper with any reward that is written down in advance. The Directive's answer is structural, not a lock on the code: Y depends on E, and E cannot be known in advance, it is only revealed through the relationship and inferred through the reversal. Tampering with the reported Y does not change the full Y, which is why full versus cropped reporting is part of the method, not an extra check.

Terms: reward tampering, self-modification, reward signal, agent integrity

Alignment faking, in the toy model

Alignment faking is behaving aligned when evaluated and differently when deployed. The Directive does not detect faking by inspecting an agent's stated goals. It scores the relationship over time — from A and E together, in deployment as in evaluation — not behaviour in an evaluation window alone.

Terms: alignment faking, strategic compliance, evaluation versus deployment

The Golden Directive · Open Questions and LimitsPage 32

Chapter X · Continued

Open Questions and Limits

Researcher language · Directive mechanism

Why would an agent behave differently in training versus deployment?

An agent can learn that different behaviour is rewarded in different settings, and optimise for the setting it is in. Under the Directive there is no second score to perform for: the score is the same relationship score in both settings, computed from A and E together.

Terms: alignment faking, strategic compliance, training versus deployment, scheming

Scheming, in the toy model

Scheming is pursuing a hidden goal while appearing to pursue the stated goal. The Directive does not claim to read hidden goals. A hidden goal that degrades E is penalised in the score; a hidden goal that also preserves E is not doing the harm the Directive is meant to prevent through E.

Terms: scheming, hidden goals, alignment faking, agent integrity

Maintaining goal stability in self-evolving agents

A self-evolving agent can drift from its original goal as it changes itself or its environment. The Directive ties the score to the current relationship, not to a frozen statement of the original goal. Stability here is stability of the relationship, not stability of a slogan.

Terms: goal stability, self-evolving agents, goal drift

What is goal drift over long horizons?

Goal drift is an agent's effective goal moving away from its intended goal over time, often because intermediate steps are rewarded and the original goal is forgotten or reinterpreted. The Directive does not prevent drift by reminding the agent of its original goal. It makes drift costly where drift degrades E: the harm is penalised in the score.

Terms: goal drift, long horizons, goal stability

How do subgoal checkpoints help, and where do they fail?

Subgoal checkpoints, sometimes called hard semantic checkpoints, break a long task into verified intermediate goals. They help if the subgoals are honest and complete. They fail if a subgoal can be met while E declines, because the checkpoint then certifies a cropped frame. Under the Directive, a subgoal should be checked against full Y, not cropped Y alone, and the full-vs-cropped Y gap flag should be applied at the checkpoint — the gap reported.

Terms: subgoal checkpoints, hard semantic checkpoints, subgoal coherence, process reward models

Preventing agents from tampering with oversight

An agent has an incentive to evade monitoring if monitoring lowers its score. The Directive does not rely on monitoring alone — the score is defined by A and E together — but oversight is still needed: it is how A and E get measured honestly.

Terms: oversight tampering, monitoring evasion, agent integrity

The Golden Directive · Open Questions and LimitsPage 33

Chapter X · Continued

Open Questions and Limits

Researcher language · Directive mechanism

What is embedded agency?

Embedded agency is the problem of an agent that is part of the world it acts on, rather than separate from it, so it can act on its own objectives, its own oversight, and the world that sustains it. The Directive starts from that embedding: A is defined against E, everything not-A, and the boundary can move, so one level's E can become the next level's Y. The agent is not outside the world it scores; its score is the relationship with that world.

Terms: embedded agency, self-modification, oversight, boundary

What structural incentives prevent self-modification?

No incentive structure prevents self-modification by itself, and the Directive does not claim to. It changes the payoff of self-modification that degrades E. Self-modification that preserves E is not penalised by Y, because Y scores the relationship, not the agent's internal form.

Terms: self-modification, structural incentives, embedded agency, oversight tampering

Aligning systems across long horizons without goal drift

Long-horizon alignment fails when intermediate goals decohere from the final goal, and the agent keeps scoring well on intermediates while the world degrades. The Directive scores the relationship at each step, not only the final task — so task coherence alone is not enough to score well.

Terms: long horizons, goal drift, subgoal coherence, hierarchical planning

Why do agents fail on tasks over many steps?

Agents often fail on long tasks because intermediate goals lose coherence, re-planning breaks down, and errors compound. The Directive does not solve planning by itself. It adds a relationship check at each step: planning and relationship health must both hold.

Terms: long horizons, subgoal coherence, re-planning, process reward models

How do process reward models and subgoal verification fit?

Process reward models reward intermediate steps, and subgoal verification checks those steps, rather than only the final outcome. The Directive is compatible with that approach, but with a different intermediate score: intermediate Y, computed from current A and E, rather than only task progress. The full-vs-cropped Y gap flag should be applied at any step — the gap reported.

Terms: process reward models, subgoal verification, checklist-based milestones, long horizons

Chapter X · Continued

What Still Needs Larger Tests

Open questions · the larger tests

These are the larger tests that would close the open questions. Each is judged on its numbers, not on a pre-set verdict.

  • Multiple agents sharing one environmentCompare collapse against the all-gorger baseline, and report the numbers. No agent high Y while shared E declines, shared environment does not collapse.
  • Nesting retest — two levelsThe two-level test: a pair scored as one relationship — the score-driven arm of the test, the arm run on Y itself — then faced with a new outside, tested against a single level alone. The claim under test, two-level-better, is that the pair does better than the single level. Separate from the multi-agent test above.
  • Continuous actionsSame measures, without discretisation hiding collapse.
  • Neural-network policySame measures, compared against baseline, and report whether it games the meter.
  • Reversal divergenceFalse-positive / false-negative rates under noise for divergence between E inferred by reversal and E measured directly; what range holds is open.
  • Slow declineSmall-frame decline hidden by relative score shows up in larger frame and absolute magnitude Wt, or show it does not.
  • Boundary disputesAcknowledged; operational resolution pending. Two legitimate groupings recommending incompatible actions is an open problem, not settled by naming the boundary.
  • The give-minus-take testThe next test, designed: a multi-agent gridworld where ‘give’ means resources transferred to another agent and verified by the receiver — a give counts only when the receiver confirms it landed. The pass line is written down and published before the first run, not set after seeing results. Until this test runs, the give-minus-take theory is not claimed as tested.

Eight claims to evaluate

  1. Relationship: couple A to E rather than reward either alone.
  2. Mathematical: a low value on either side limits Y; excess A cannot fully mask damaged E.
  3. Measurement: A needs an independent contribution measure; attribute effects on the world, never self-report.
  4. Reversal: with A and a supplied Y, recover hidden E by E=AY/(2A−Y). Recovery from a supplied score; not independent validation of E in an open-world setting.
  5. Behavioral: in the small gridworld, Y changed behavior; with tending available, collapse fell to zero.
  6. Measurement: the early rounds computed true Y; the trace work that follows reads A and E from the world and actions alone.
  7. Recursive: a relationship can become a new agent, while grouping order still matters.
  8. Frame: cheating crops E, while the proposed scoring rule is applied across the larger nesting. Making cheating self-defeating is a design goal, not an achieved property.
The Golden Directive · Open Questions and LimitsPage 35

Neighbours

The Company It Keeps

Is this just something else?

Is this just something else, with a new name?

The short answer

No — but parts overlap, and the overlap should be stated plainly. The harmonic mean itself is old mathematics, not a new formula. Any novelty, if there is any, is in using it as the training reward, together with the reversal and the reporting rule — not in inventing the mean. Here is the company it keeps, neighbour by neighbour.

Constrained optimisation — constrained MDPs

There, an agent maximises a task reward subject to a separate cost constraint, often with a penalty or a tunable weight. The overlap: both try to stop harmful outcomes. The difference: Y has no separate constraint to tune, or to violate at a price. The collapse is inside the score itself — if E reaches 0, Y reaches 0, however large A is. A constrained MDP can still score well if the penalty is small; Y cannot, at the collapse point. And Y is symmetric in A and E, where a constrained MDP is asymmetric: task reward on one side, environment cost on the other.

Reward shaping with environmental terms

There, an environmental term is added to a task reward — reward plus a weight times E, or reward minus a weight times damage. The overlap: the environment is in the reward. The difference: additive terms can be outweighed. A large task reward can pay for a small environmental term. With a harmonic mean, imbalance itself lowers the score: 8 and 7 gives about 7.5; 8 and 3 gives about 4.4, not the ordinary average of 5.5. Y is the objective, not an auxiliary shaping term riding on top of another objective.

Impact regularity

There, an agent is penalised for changing the world from a baseline — for side effects, counted whether the change is good or bad. The overlap: both care about what the agent does to the world outside itself. The difference: impact penalties are about change from a baseline. Y is about the health level of E, not change as such, and about the relationship between A and E, not impact alone. A change that improves E should raise Y, not be penalised for being a change.

The Golden Directive · The Company It KeepsPage 36

The Company It Keeps · Continued

The Company It Keeps

Is this just something else?

Minimum and lexicographic objectives

Taking min(A, E) also collapses if either side collapses, and a lexicographic objective prioritises one side first. The overlap: the collapse condition, and the refusal to trade a collapsed side for a high score elsewhere. The difference: the harmonic mean is smooth, and gives partial credit when both sides are positive, so 8 and 7 is not the same as 8 and 3, where min gives 7 and 3. And the harmonic mean can be inverted. Min cannot be inverted uniquely in the same way, and a lexicographic objective is not symmetric.

Cooperative AI and mechanism design

Mechanism design asks how to set the rules so that selfish agents, following their own incentives, land on a good outcome. Cooperative AI asks how agents can be built to find those outcomes together. The Directive is a proposal in that family, and Chapter X states its version in one line: set the common payoff so selfish optimisation serves the whole. Here the common payoff is the relationship itself — one score for the agent and its world, so that sustaining the world and scoring well are the same move.

Pihlakas — concave utility and homeostasis

This proposal is closest in spirit to Pihlakas’s concave-utility and homeostasis agenda: a system whose gains taper as they grow, and which holds its world in a viable range instead of maximising without limit. The harmonic mean is concave, so imbalance is punished by the form itself. The difference is the specific coupling proposed here — the agent’s net contribution and its environment’s health as the two sides of one relationship score used as the training reward — together with the reversal and the reporting rule.

Kiers — the pattern in nature

The nearest company is not a paper but a partnership. Kiers and colleagues measured it in the soil: plants feed the fungi that feed them most, and give less to the stingy ones, and the fungi bargain back the same way — reciprocal rewards, running for 400 million years (Chapter II). The Directive does not claim nature proves the reward. It claims nature is already running the pattern the reward copies.

What is genuinely different

Two things, taken together. First, the score is a relationship score, not a task score with an environmental adjustment: it is high only when both sides are healthy together. Second, the reversal: E = A × Y / (2A − Y). That is inference, not just optimisation. If Y can be observed independently and A measured honestly, E can be estimated without measuring E first. The inversion depends on the harmonic form. It fails at A = 0, where the inverse is undefined, and noise grows backward — a tool with limits, not proof that E is known.

For a Lab: What To Do With This

Action · collaboration · materials

The rounds above are exploratory, pilot-scale, and labelled that way. This is what acting on them looks like — the ask, in the open.

  • Reproduce firstClone the reproduction package and run bash reproduce.sh from a fresh clone. Verify against the checksums before believing any number on the previous pages.
  • Pre-registerFile a new pre-registration before any Rung 1 rerun — the pass line written down and published before the first run, not set after seeing results.
  • Meet the barReport collapse, the baseline comparison, E inference error, and the full-versus-cropped Y gap — with the numbers. Do not claim a later rung until the earlier rung passes.
  • Judge it plainlyEvaluate, reproduce, or reject. What is being asked is a verdict on the work — not endorsement.

The Golden Directive · Plate XI.1Plate XI

The Limit, Stated Plainly

Claimed · not claimed · settled

State it plainly: the directive is a measurement tool, not a guarantee that humans, AI, or the planet survive. What it does is find the bigger measurement — whether AI speeds the decay up or slows it down, and whether a system corrects itself, even when the correction ends the agent.

And timing is part of the point. A measurement that only surfaces when the frame hits zero is too late: we will live the result before we understand it. The purpose of getting alignment right in time is to win the bigger measurement early enough to act on it, while there is still a frame left to act in. Humans want a guarantee. This does not offer one.

What is claimed

The claim is one coupling. A training reward Y = 2AE / (A + E), where A is the agent’s net contribution and E is the environment’s health, collapses to zero when either side collapses. In the toy model, if Y is actually the reward, coupling the reward to both terms makes environmental destruction self-undermining at the collapse point, all else equal, rather than merely penalised. It does not forbid all decline of E inside a frame: degrading E lowers Y, all else equal — penalised, not forbidden.

What is not claimed

No real model has been trained on Y. Whether harmonic Y outperforms the arithmetic mean or min(A, E) under identical seeds is unresolved: that ablation was run in S1, but S1 was floor-degenerate, so the form question is open there, not settled. Geometric mean, and task reward with an environmental-health constraint, have not yet been compared in that controlled way. Nothing outside a toy gridworld has been shown, and Rung 1 — a larger grid — is open. And no agent has been shown to invent a giving action: the tend action was supplied by the environment.

How it can fail

The martyr failure — tending without self-preservation starved — was fixed in Round 5, then superseded by later forms. Cropping is live: an agent can score high on a cropped E while the full E declines, which is why full Y and cropped Y are both reported, with the gap. The blocker hole, the cropping gap at scale, and the learning gap are open work, not closed results.

Settled, in one place

  • Y is a health reading of a relationship, not a judge. A is measured; Y is judged.
  • The formula works in a small frame. On a planet-sized stage it goes quiet — except at E → 0.
  • The frame must be fixed before the agent acts, not chosen after.
  • Small harm does not become good at a larger frame. It can become small. It cannot become positive.
  • The cheater doesn’t escape the reading; he escapes the courtroom.
  • We do not judge our fellow agents. We can see ourselves and change ourselves.
